# The Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models {#irt-models}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain what a latent trait is and why IRT puts people and items on the
  same scale;
* write down the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models and say what each parameter does
  to the item characteristic curve;
* fit the three models with `mirt()` and read their parameters in the
  traditional IRT metric;
* describe an item in words from its curve.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[item response theory](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-response-theory),
[latent trait](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#latent-trait),
[logit](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#logit),
[Rasch model](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#rasch-model),
[2PL](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#two-pl),
[3PL](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#three-pl),
[item characteristic curve](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-characteristic-curve),
[difficulty](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#difficulty),
[discrimination](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#discrimination),
[guessing](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#guessing),
[slope-intercept form](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#slope-intercept).

## The ideas

IRT assumes that a person's responses depend on an unobserved **latent
trait** $\theta$ (theta): ability, knowledge, an attitude. By convention
$\theta$ has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 in the calibration group, so a
person at $\theta = 1$ is one standard deviation above average.

Each item gets an **item characteristic curve** (ICC): the probability of a
correct answer as a function of $\theta$. The three classic models differ in
how many parameters shape that curve [@hambleton1991; @embretson2000].

**The Rasch (1PL) model** has one parameter per item, the difficulty $b_j$:

$$P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i) = \frac{\exp(\theta_i - b_j)}{1 + \exp(\theta_i - b_j)}.$$

The difficulty is the point on the $\theta$ scale where the probability is
0.5. All curves have the same slope, so they never cross, and the sum score
contains all the information about $\theta$.

**The two-parameter logistic (2PL) model** adds a discrimination $a_j$:

$$P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i) = \frac{\exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}{1 + \exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}.$$

A larger $a_j$ gives a steeper curve: the item separates people just below
$b_j$ from people just above it more sharply. Values between about 0.8 and 2.5
are typical for good achievement items; values below about 0.5 mean the item
hardly tells people apart.

**The three-parameter logistic (3PL) model** adds a lower asymptote $c_j$,
often called the guessing parameter:

$$P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i) = c_j + (1 - c_j)\frac{\exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}{1 + \exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}.$$

Even very low-ability people get a multiple-choice item right with
probability $c_j$, roughly one over the number of options if they guess at
random. With a lower asymptote, $b_j$ is where the probability is
$(1 + c_j)/2$ rather than 0.5.

mirt estimates the models in **slope-intercept form**,
$a_j\theta_i + d_j$, which behaves better numerically. The two forms are
related by $b_j = -d_j / a_j$. Use `coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE)`, or
mirtverse's `tidy()` (which uses `IRTpars = TRUE` by default), to see $a$ and
$b$.

## Example 1: the LSAT section 7 items

`LSAT7` holds the response patterns of 1,000 people to five items from a
section of the Law School Admission Test, stored as a frequency table.
`expand.table()` turns it into one row per person.

```{r data-irt-models-1}
# Five dichotomous LSAT items, one row per test taker.
resp <- expand.table(LSAT7)
```

We fit the three models. `itemtype` chooses the model and `verbose = FALSE`
hides the iteration history.

```{r}
rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
twopl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL",   verbose = FALSE)
threepl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE)
```

The item parameters in the IRT metric:

```{r}
coef(twopl, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
```

The columns `g` and `u` are the lower and upper asymptotes, fixed at 0 and 1
for the 2PL. The same information as a tidy table, ready for a report:

```{r}
tidy(twopl)
```

All five items have negative difficulties: this is an easy section for this
group. Item 3 has the steepest slope, items 4 and 5 the flattest. The curves
show it at a glance.

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
gg_trace(twopl, facet = FALSE)
```

Compare the Rasch curves, which are parallel by construction, with the 2PL
curves, which are not:

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
library(patchwork)
(gg_trace(rasch, facet = FALSE) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Rasch")) +
  (gg_trace(twopl, facet = FALSE) + ggplot2::ggtitle("2PL")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

The 3PL adds a lower asymptote for each item. With only five easy items there
is very little information about what low-ability people do. Look at the $c$
estimates (`g`) and their confidence intervals:

```{r}
threepl_se <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
tidy(threepl_se, conf.int = TRUE) |> subset(term == "g")
```

Four of the five lower asymptotes sit at essentially zero, on the boundary
of the parameter space, and the one that does not (Item 2) has a confidence
interval that runs from almost 0 to well over 0.5. The data say very little
about guessing. Which model should we report? That is a question for Chapter
\@ref(estimation). For now, notice that a model with more parameters is not
automatically better: it has to be supported by the data.

`interpret()` describes the fitted model in plain language. Its *Items*
section is a useful check on your own reading of the curves.

```{r}
interpret(twopl)
```

## Example 2: a driving theory test with guessing

To see when the 3PL matters, we simulate a 20-item driving theory test with
four options per question, taken by 3,000 learner drivers. Because we
simulate, we know the true parameters and can check how well each model
recovers them.

```{r data-irt-models-2}
# Simulated 20-item, four-option test with real guessing (c around 0.2).
set.seed(202)
n_items <- 20
true <- data.frame(a = rlnorm(n_items, 0.2, 0.25),
                   b = seq(-1.5, 2, length.out = n_items),
                   c = rbeta(n_items, 5, 17))
resp <- simdata(a = matrix(true$a), d = matrix(-true$a * true$b),
                N = 3000, itemtype = "3PL", guess = true$c)
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("D%02d", 1:n_items)
```

The data chunk converts the true $b$ into an intercept with $d = -ab$,
because `simdata()` uses the slope-intercept form.

```{r}
fit2 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
fit3 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE)
est2 <- coef(fit2, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
est3 <- coef(fit3, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
recovery <- data.frame(
  model = rep(c("2PL", "3PL"), each = 2),
  parameter = rep(c("a", "b"), 2),
  bias = c(mean(est2[, "a"] - true$a), mean(est2[, "b"] - true$b),
           mean(est3[, "a"] - true$a), mean(est3[, "b"] - true$b)),
  rmse = c(sqrt(mean((est2[, "a"] - true$a)^2)), sqrt(mean((est2[, "b"] - true$b)^2)),
           sqrt(mean((est3[, "a"] - true$a)^2)), sqrt(mean((est3[, "b"] - true$b)^2))))
recovery
```

When people really do guess, the 2PL absorbs the guessing into the other
parameters: it **underestimates discrimination** and makes hard items look
**easier** than they are. The 3PL recovers the parameters much better, and its
lower asymptotes are close to the truth on average:

```{r}
c(mean_true_c = mean(true$c), mean_estimated_c = mean(est3[, "g"]))
```

The empirical item curve makes the problem visible. For the hardest item,
the observed proportions correct for low-ability groups sit well above the
2PL curve, which heads towards zero:

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
gg_empirical(fit2, "D20") + gg_empirical(fit3, "D20")
```

**What to take away.** The 3PL is worth its extra parameters when items can
be answered by guessing *and* there are enough low-ability test takers to
estimate the lower asymptote: here 3,000 people and a range of difficulties.
With small samples or easy tests, $c$ is poorly determined, and a 2PL (or a
3PL with a prior on $c$) is often the safer choice.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Using the 2PL for `LSAT7`, compute by hand the probability that a person
   at $\theta = -1$ answers Item 3 correctly. Check your answer with
   `probtrace(extract.item(twopl, 3), -1)`.
2. Fit the Rasch model to `LSAT7` and compare its difficulties with the 2PL
   difficulties. Which item moves most, and why?
3. In Example 2, refit the 3PL using only the first 300 test takers. What
   happens to the recovery of $c$?
4. Sketch (on paper) the curve of an item with $a = 0.3$ and $b = 0$. Would you
   keep this item on a test used to award licences?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
p <- coef(twopl, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
plogis(p["Item.3", "a"] * (-1 - p["Item.3", "b"]))
probtrace(extract.item(twopl, 3), matrix(-1))

pr <- coef(rasch, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
round(cbind(rasch = pr[, "b"], twopl = p[, "b"]), 2)

small <- mirt(resp[1:300, ], 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE)
summary(coef(small, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"] - true$c)
```

2. Items whose 2PL slope is far from the common Rasch slope move most, here
   Item 3 (the steepest) and Item 5 (one of the flattest). A flat
   item (small $a$) has a 2PL difficulty further from zero, because its curve
   only reaches 0.5 far out on the scale.
3. You may first see a warning that the EM algorithm stopped after 500
   cycles: the 3PL is hard to estimate in small samples (Chapter
   \@ref(estimation)). With 300 people the $c$ estimates scatter much more widely around the
   truth, and some may be close to 0 or implausibly large. The estimates of
   $a$ and $b$ get worse too, because the three parameters trade off.
4. The curve is almost flat: the chance of a correct answer barely depends on
   ability. Such an item adds little information and some noise; it should
   go back to the item writers.

</details>

models for a real-sized certification exam and to defend your choice to the
board. Chapter \@ref(estimation) gives you the tools for that comparison.

## Further reading {-}

Embretson and Reise [-@embretson2000] give an accessible introduction for
psychologists; Hambleton, Swaminathan and Rogers [-@hambleton1991] a short
classic; de Ayala [-@deayala2022] a thorough modern treatment. Chalmers
[-@chalmers2012] describes the mirt package.
